summary: A [National Digital Strategy](2025-09-22 Namibia to build national data centre under 2025-2029 digital strategy) was published in August 2025 and a [ministry strategic plan and ICT policy](2026-01-29-ict-ministry-launches-strategic-plan-policy-namibian) launched in January 2026, with neither text held.
developments:
The digital strategy is in force and the national data centre it calls for was still at concept-note stage a month after publication; the document itself is not held and two sources give its period differently ([strategy](2025-09-22 Namibia to build national data centre under 2025-2029 digital strategy), [readiness](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc)).

The ministry's strategic plan and national ICT policy were launched at Opuwo in January 2026, prioritising affordable broadband and mobile coverage in rural and underserved areas, cybersecurity, data protection and electronic government, and naming high data costs, limited infrastructure and unequal access as the barriers; neither document text is held ([plan](2026-01-29-ict-ministry-launches-strategic-plan-policy-namibian)).

summary: A [national artificial-intelligence strategy](2026-08-05-namibia-deloitte-ai-strategy-framework) is in development through the [research council working group](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc), guided by a completed [readiness assessment](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc).
developments:
Consultations began under the council's working group and its technical advisory committees; no draft is published, and the ministry states the strategy is sequenced ahead of legislation ([strategy](2026-08-05-namibia-deloitte-ai-strategy-framework), [framework](2026-08-05-namibia-deloitte-ai-strategy), [coordination](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc)).

The working group is a multi-stakeholder platform with science, data and skills committees and runs the national strategy process ([group](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc)).

A readiness assessment was completed by the council with the education ministry and an international body, and its findings were restated by the authors in February 2026; the report itself is not held ([assessment](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc)).

progress: No change, announced as following the strategy with nothing drafted or tabled
summary: [Artificial-intelligence legislation](2026-08-05-namibia-deloitte-ai-strategy-framework) is announced as following the strategy, and the research council's own authors recorded no governance framework in place.
developments:
The minister sequenced legislation behind the strategy, and nothing has been drafted or tabled ([sequencing](2026-08-05-namibia-deloitte-ai-strategy-framework), [framework](2026-08-05-namibia-deloitte-ai-strategy)).

The research council's own authors recorded no artificial-intelligence governance framework in place as at February 2026. A strategy that is itself unpublished cannot yet ground a statute, so both halves of the governance question are pending on the same document.

summary: The [Data Protection Bill](2025-08-14-govt-to-introduce-data-protection-bill-september-namibian) has not been tabled about thirteen years after drafting began, and the [March 2022 draft](2022-03-01-namibia-draft-data-protection-bill-revised-version-mict) remains the last version published for comment.
developments:
A tabling was announced for September 2025 ([announcement](2025-08-14-govt-to-introduce-data-protection-bill-september-namibian), [return](2025-08-17-data-protection-bill-returns-to-parliament-namibiansun)) and the bill was still in finalisation in August 2026, with no data-protection statute in force ([finalisation](2026-07-14-namibia-pushes-cyber-security-reforms-itweb), [concerns](2026-08-04-namibia-mp-data-control-concerns-china-smart-city-grant)).

The March 2022 revised draft runs to fifty-nine pages and eight Parts, with the supervisory authority at Part 2 ([draft](2022-03-01-namibia-draft-data-protection-bill-revised-version-mict)).

The 2020 version carries a Part on rights of the data subject, together with Parts on recourse to the judicial authority and on offences and penalties, none of which appears in the 2022 version, where access and correction survive only as controller obligations ([2020 version](2020-01-01-namibia-draft-data-protection-bill-2020-version), [removal](2025-08-17-data-protection-bill-returns-to-parliament-namibiansun)).

summary: A [Cybercrime Bill](2026-07-14-namibia-pushes-cyber-security-reforms-itweb) was named as being finalised in July 2026, with no draft published and no tabling date given.
developments:
Enforcement has relied on the electronic transactions statute, the communications statute and the penal code; cabinet approved cybercrime proposals in November 2025 ([proposals](2025-11-21-namibia-cabinet-approves-cyber-crime-proposals-itweb)) and the minister named the bill as being finalised alongside the data protection bill in July 2026 ([finalisation](2026-07-14-namibia-pushes-cyber-security-reforms-itweb)).

The base first names this bill in July 2026, and the national incident response team states in its own report that it cannot fully execute its mandate absent a cybersecurity law.

summary: The [Electronic Transactions Act 2019](2023-01-01 Digital Trade Regulatory Integration - Namibia Country Profile) has been in force since March 2021 and covers signatures, consumer protection and contracts but not personal data or cross-border flow.
developments:
The Act is the interim instrument law enforcement relies on for cybercrime, with the communications statute and the penal code ([Act](2026-07-14-namibia-pushes-cyber-security-reforms-itweb)).

A regulatory profile records that it does not reach cross-border data flow, data localisation or personal data protection ([profile](2023-01-01 Digital Trade Regulatory Integration - Namibia Country Profile)). Company process under the corporate laws reform is routed through it, so it is doing more work than it was written for.

summary: The [Access to Information Act 8 of 2022](2022-12-28-namibia-access-to-information-act-8-of-2022) is gazetted and not commenced, and no Information Commissioner has been appointed.
developments:
Section 86 leaves commencement to a date determined by the minister, no commencement notice is held, and the Act runs to ten Parts and eighty-six sections whose compliance deadlines run from commencement ([Act](2022-12-28-namibia-access-to-information-act-8-of-2022)).

Appointment machinery for the Commissioner and Deputy was itself gazetted in December 2024, setting five-year selection committee terms and a five-member quorum, made ahead of the Act's own commencement, so the annual report the Act requires cannot yet exist ([regulations](2024-12-09-namibia-information-commissioner-appointment-regulations)).

summary: The [Civil Registration and Identification Act 13 of 2024](2024-12-30 Civil Registration and Identification Act, 2024) is the statutory basis for a single civil register and a unique identity number, and a [gazette notice withdrawing older documents](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026) has not issued.
developments:
The Act was assented in December 2024 as the basis for a single civil register, a unique identity number and identity-data confidentiality, and was read by officials in July 2026 as permitting institutions to accept either the physical card or its digital version, with disclosure conditional on the holder's consent; the commencement date is not established in this base ([Act](2024-12-30 Civil Registration and Identification Act, 2024), [reading](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026)).

The notice that will end the validity of pre-independence cards, older documents and current machine-readable cards has not issued, so until it does the September 2026 card is additive rather than replacing anything ([notice](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026)).

summary: A [Data Protection Supervisory Authority](2022-03-01-namibia-draft-data-protection-bill-revised-version-mict) sits at Part 2 of a draft bill that has not been tabled, and no authority exists.
developments:
The draft's stated objects are establishing the authority with its own powers and duties, obligations on controllers and processors, rights for data subjects, and codes of conduct ([draft](2022-03-01-namibia-draft-data-protection-bill-revised-version-mict), [earlier version](2020-01-01-namibia-draft-data-protection-bill-2020-version)).

A civil-society critique of the 2022 consultation argued the sections on the authority's independence need substantial redrafting. Four years on there is no authority, no commencement and no later text.

summary: Memoranda were signed with [Angola](2026-06-11-namibia-and-angola-join-forces-angotic-mou) and [Botswana](2026-08-10-namibia-botswana-trans-kalahari-4g-mou), and cabinet [authorised signature with the Republic of Congo](2026-07-27-namibia-cabinet-approves-ict-mou-with-congo).
developments:
The Angolan memorandum covers joint events, exchange of expertise and cybersecurity, with no amount or instrument named ([Angola](2026-06-11-namibia-and-angola-join-forces-angotic-mou)).

The Botswana memorandum was signed at Kasane in August 2026 between the two ministries with their operators and regulators, covering digital transformation, cybersecurity, connectivity and skills; the two sides costed the corridor's remaining 4G gaps at about N$52 million across thirteen new sites and recorded a completed cross-border fibre link, the first direct one between the operators ([Botswana](2026-08-10-namibia-botswana-trans-kalahari-4g-mou), [cooperation](2026-08-07-botswana-namibia-ict-cooperation-mou)).

Cabinet approved a memorandum with the Republic of Congo and authorised the minister to sign, with no scope, financing or signature date published ([Congo](2026-07-27-namibia-cabinet-approves-ict-mou-with-congo)).

summary: The regional regulators' [legal and policy committee](2026-08-11-techreviewafrica-crasa-legal-policy-committee-ai-data-governance) first met at Windhoek in August 2026, and the minister holds a [seat on an international artificial-intelligence commission](2026-07-31-gsma-atlas-umoja-ai-launch).
developments:
The committee was constituted and met with artificial-intelligence governance, data governance and protection, digital public infrastructure and regional regulatory harmonisation on its agenda, hosted by the national regulator; no work programme, output or timetable is published ([committee](2026-08-11-techreviewafrica-crasa-legal-policy-committee-ai-data-governance)).

The ICT minister is one of eight Africans on a forty-four member commission, on the convening body's account ([seat](2026-07-31-gsma-atlas-umoja-ai-launch), [declaration](2026-07-24-gsma-abuja-declaration-meaningful-connectivity-atlas-umoja)).

summary: A [master service agreement](2026-06-15-telecom-namibia-angola-telecom-satcab-sarssy-1tbps) with two Angolan counterparts commits [1.0 Tbps of dedicated capacity](2026-06-15-telecom-namibia-angola-telecom-satcab-sarssy-1tbps), and a [satellite pilot](2026-06-12-namibia-angola-ink-satellite-deal-itweb) is running.
developments:
The agreement was signed in June 2026 by the state fixed operator with two Angolan counterparts, with the Namibian operator as landing party hosting Angolan equipment, covering design, integration, testing, commissioning and handover; it builds on a memorandum and commercial terms agreed in April 2026 ([agreement](2026-06-15-telecom-namibia-angola-telecom-satcab-sarssy-1tbps), [deals](2026-06-15 Telecom Namibia signs more satellite, subsea connectivity deals with Angola firms)).

Initial dedicated transmission capacity on the subsea system is fixed at 1.0 Tbps by that agreement, as stated by the parties, with no delivered figure held ([capacity](2026-06-15-telecom-namibia-angola-telecom-satcab-sarssy-1tbps)).

A pilot commercial agreement between the state fixed operator and Angola's space agency is running, with full commercial launch targeted after the pilot ([pilot](2026-06-12-namibia-angola-ink-satellite-deal-itweb)).

summary: The [2022 consultation on the Data Protection Bill](2022-10-26-action-namibia-government-seeks-public-input-draft-data-protection-bill) drew a coalition submission and an independent critique, and no further consultation is on record.
developments:
The ministry opened public input in October 2022 with a closing date of 30 November; a civil-society coalition filed a submission on that date and a research institute published the same argument as a public paper in December, arguing the sections on the supervisory authority's independence need substantial redrafting and that the offences and penalties provisions are undeveloped ([consultation](2022-10-26-action-namibia-government-seeks-public-input-draft-data-protection-bill), [submission](2022-11-30-action-namibia-coalition-civil-society-submission-data-protection-bill-2021), [critique](2022-12-14-ippr-data-protection-bill-not-fit-for-purpose)).

No ministry-published list of respondents is held and no further consultation activity is on record since. A separate three-year memorandum between the regulator and the chamber of commerce takes legislative reform as a joint workstream with a business lobby, which the instrument does not address ([memorandum](2026-07-30-namibia-ncci-cran-mou-digital-economy-pki-cybersecurity)).

summary: The regulator states it is the [national root certification authority](2026-07-29-namibia-eid-community-outreach-omaheke-undp), and the [interbank settlement system migrated](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking) to the international messaging standard.
developments:
The regulator states it anchors the digital trust framework and regulates certificate and certification-service providers, a role the ministry had exercised in accrediting electronic-signature providers under the 2019 statute; that places the trust anchor inside the communications regulator rather than a separate cyber agency ([authority](2026-07-29-namibia-eid-community-outreach-omaheke-undp), [accreditation](2025-09-17-ai-abuse-overshadows-namibia-e-signature-drive-itweb)).

The interbank settlement system has migrated to the ISO 20022 messaging standard ([migration](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking), [pact](2026-07-02-bon-ipn-namclear-instant-payments-pact-techafricanews)).

progress: Mixed, a universal service levy in force and a fund disbursing while the fund's own seed figure is unreconciled and the regulator ran a loss
summary: A [universal service levy](2024-09-27-namibia-gg-8455-gn-559-regulations-prescribing-universal-service-levy) of up to 0.5 per cent of turnover has been in force since 2024, and the [Universal Service Fund](2025-03-19-thebrief-namibia-universal-service-fund-launch-n145-million-seed-funding) has awarded nine sites, while the [regulator turned a surplus into a loss](2025-08-07-cran-integrated-annual-report-2025).
developments:
The levy is not to exceed 0.5 per cent of annual turnover per licensee with a flat N$500 floor for non-profit licensees, invoiced on audited statements and payable within thirty days into the fund ([regulations](2024-09-27-namibia-gg-8455-gn-559-regulations-prescribing-universal-service-levy)); an amendment let the fund receive donations or grants, which is what makes government funding receivable ([regulations](2024-09-27-namibia-gg-8455-gn-559-regulations-prescribing-universal-service-levy), [withdrawal](2024-06-21-namibia-gg-8384-cran-universal-service-levy-withdrawal-and-notice-of-intention)). A gap analysis identifies 119 locations that will remain unserved after coverage obligations, of which government funding covers the capital cost of 42 ([analysis](2024-01-01-cran-revised-universal-access-and-gap-analysis-report-2024)).

The fund launched in March 2025 and a first bidding round awarded nine sites with almost N$31 million of capital subsidy across the five regions where 4G coverage is below 80 per cent, with free internet for schools and clinics on those sites for seven years ([fund](2025-03-19-thebrief-namibia-universal-service-fund-launch-n145-million-seed-funding), [priority](2026-02-02 Namibian regulator proposes tax breaks on 4G devices), [report](2025-08-07-cran-integrated-annual-report-2025)). The government commitment is given as N$115,000,000 in the regulator's own report and N$145,000,000 in the launch reporting, and the two are not reconciled ([launch](2025-06-04 Namibia targets 100% telecom coverage nationwide by 2030)).

The regulator's revenue fell 23 per cent to 15.5 per cent below budget while operating expenditure rose 42 per cent, turning a N$32.8 million surplus into a N$25.5 million loss ([accounts](2025-08-07-cran-integrated-annual-report-2025), [prior year](2024-09-06-cran-integrated-annual-report-2024)).

progress: Mixed, 5G live in three centres and 2G and 3G ordered retired while the regulator's own published series stops at 2023
summary: [4G population coverage was 88.4 per cent on 2023 data](2024-11-01-cran-ict-sector-market-report-2023), [commercial 5G is live in three centres](2026-02-10-towards-5g-enabled-digitalized-namibia-2026-telecomreviewafrica), and operators have been [instructed to retire 2G and 3G](2026-08-20-namibian-sun-mtc-smartphone-subsidies-2g-3g-shutdown).
developments:
The regulator's series gives 4G population coverage of 85 per cent in 2022, with six of fourteen regions below 80 per cent and one at 41 per cent, 456 of 1,380 schools and 84 of 452 health facilities without 4G coverage, and about 2,000,000 of 2,900,000 mobile cards actively used for internet ([2022](2023-12-01-cran-ict-sector-market-report-2022)); the 2023 edition gives coverage of 88.4 per cent, fibre to the home at 27 per cent of fixed broadband subscribers and a 6 per cent fall in active cards ([2023](2024-11-01-cran-ict-sector-market-report-2023), [release](2024-12-13-cran-media-release-unveils-2023-ict-sector-report)). The published series is irregular and no edition reporting 2024 data is held ([series](2024-11-01-cran-ict-sector-market-report-2023)).

Commercial 5G launched at the end of August 2025 in three centres, with nationwide deployment stated as phased and city-first ([5G](2026-02-10-towards-5g-enabled-digitalized-namibia-2026-telecomreviewafrica)).

The regulator has instructed operators to retire 2G and 3G and refarm the spectrum; the incumbent asked government to subsidise smartphones before switch-off, and no switch-off date or government response is on file ([retirement](2026-08-20-namibian-sun-mtc-smartphone-subsidies-2g-3g-shutdown)).

progress: No change, a regulator proposal with no fiscal instrument or ministerial response behind it
summary: The regulator's chief executive [proposed tax relief on fourth-generation devices](2026-02-02 Namibian regulator proposes tax breaks on 4G devices), against operator-reported tower utilisation close to half in one region.
developments:
The proposal was made at a tower launch in Kunene; no fiscal instrument, budget line or ministerial response has been published, and the operator reported utilisation close to 50 per cent across about 74 enabled towers in the region ([proposal](2026-02-02 Namibian regulator proposes tax breaks on 4G devices)).

Device cost, not coverage, is what the proposal treats as the constraint, and the incumbent made the same argument a year later in asking for smartphone subsidies before the 2G and 3G switch-off.

summary: A [satellite licence application was declined](2026-06-22-namibia-cran-dismisses-starlink-appeals-sia) and 622 of 624 reconsideration requests failed, under a [51 per cent Namibian ownership requirement](2026-06-22-namibia-cran-dismisses-starlink-appeals-sia) the applicant cannot meet.
developments:
Licence and spectrum were declined in March 2026 on three of six statutory criteria; 622 of 624 reconsideration requests failed the legal threshold, two were refused on merits, and the operator's own request was dismissed as out of time ([dismissal](2026-06-22-namibia-cran-dismisses-starlink-appeals-sia), [rejection](2026-06-24-namibian-regulator-rejects-starlink-again-connectingafrica), [block](2026-03-26 Starlink blocked from operating in Namibia)).

The ownership requirement is in force with no exemption granted; the regulator held that wholly foreign ownership raises questions of jurisdiction, enforceability of compliance obligations and effective oversight, and states the power to waive the rule rests with the minister rather than with it ([requirement](2026-06-22-namibia-cran-dismisses-starlink-appeals-sia)). The applicant stated its global shareholding rules bar it from accepting local ownership ([exemption](2026-03-26 Starlink blocked from operating in Namibia)).

progress: No change, two commercial facilities named with no capacity, load or customer figure for either
summary: [Two commercial data centres](2026-06-15 Namibia encouraged by Angola on datacentre establishment) are named as established, one operator-run and one run by an aerospace company with a national university.
developments:
No capacity, load or customer figures are held for either facility ([facilities](2026-06-15 Namibia encouraged by Angola on datacentre establishment)).

They are the whole of the country's operating data-centre estate on this record, and the case for hosting compute in the country rests on the subsea landing rather than on installed capacity.

summary: A [national public data centre](2025-09-23-namibia-expedites-data-centre-smart-city-development-itweb) is at concept-note stage, while a [vendor-built facility for artificial-intelligence workloads](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure) is being built on a Chinese commitment.
developments:
Cabinet directed a concept note and project proposal to the ministry and the Office of the Prime Minister in September 2025, and no site, capacity, cost or date was published by August 2026; the minister said in June 2026 that Angola's national facility had encouraged the plan ([concept](2025-09-23-namibia-expedites-data-centre-smart-city-development-itweb), [proposal](2025-09-22 Namibia to build national data centre under 2025-2029 digital strategy), [encouragement](2026-06-15 Namibia encouraged by Angola on datacentre establishment)).

A vendor is building smart-city solutions and a data centre with the ICT and home affairs ministries, on a Chinese commitment of CNY 98,000,000 given by the source as about US$14.4m ([funding](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure)); no signed agreement, annexure or contractor list is held, and an opposition member gives the same commitment as N$245m ([funding](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure), [talks](2026-07-08-nandi-ndaitwah-pushes-ai-jobs-huawei-talks-namibian)).

summary: Cabinet approved a [government-sector incident response team and security operations centres](2025-11-21-namibia-cabinet-approves-cyber-crime-proposals-itweb) and a [cyber-skills programme](2025-11-21-namibia-cabinet-approves-cyber-crime-proposals-itweb) for government technology staff, neither established.
developments:
The team was approved as the central authority coordinating incidents across government, with the Office of the Prime Minister directed to coordinate phased implementation; no establishment, budget or timetable is reported ([team](2025-11-21-namibia-cabinet-approves-cyber-crime-proposals-itweb)).

Targeted training in cyber hygiene, incident response and threat intelligence was approved alongside it, with no delivery, budget or cohort reported nine months later ([training](2025-11-21-namibia-cabinet-approves-cyber-crime-proposals-itweb)).

progress: Mixed, the response team fully operational and publishing while detected vulnerabilities rose 39.8 per cent in a quarter and no cybersecurity law exists
summary: The [national incident response team](2026-07-22-namcsirt-q2-vulnerabilities) completed its three-year plan and publishes an [annual landscape report](2026-04-11-nam-csirt-namibia-cybersecurity-landscape-report-2025), while [detected vulnerabilities rose 39.8 per cent](2026-07-22-namcsirt-q2-vulnerabilities) in a quarter.
developments:
The team operates under the regulator, was officially launched in April 2025, completed Phase 3 of its implementation plan in the 2025/26 year, and joined three international and regional bodies during 2025; about US$1m is allocated to cybersecurity for 2026/27 ([team](2026-07-22-namcsirt-q2-vulnerabilities), [surge](2026-04-13-namibia-reports-37-surge-cyberattacks-2025-wearetech), [growth](2025-07-30-cyber-threats-surge-amid-namibia-digital-growth-namibiansun)).

The 2025 landscape report records 1,701,883 attack events, up about 37 per cent on 2024, and 2,231,970 vulnerabilities, with five ransomware victims ([report](2026-04-11-nam-csirt-namibia-cybersecurity-landscape-report-2025)); the country scored 36.93 on an international cybersecurity index in 2024 against 11.47 in 2020, and the team states in its own text that it cannot fully execute its mandate absent a cybersecurity law ([report](2026-04-11-nam-csirt-namibia-cybersecurity-landscape-report-2025), [inaugural](2025-01-01-nam-csirt-namibia-cyber-security-landscape-report-2024)).

Incident management guidelines came into force in April 2026 setting out detection, reporting and coordinated response ([guidelines](2026-07-23-namibia-cyber-vulnerabilities-surge-cran-namcsirt)), and detected vulnerabilities and events rose 39.8 and 56.7 per cent in the following quarter ([quarter](2026-07-22-namcsirt-q2-vulnerabilities)).

progress: No change, three interoperability systems on file and no operational statement for any of them since 2020
summary: A [governmental interoperability solution](2016-12-01 Governmental Interoperability in Namibia - E-riigi Akadeemia) delivered in 2016, a [data exchange service bus](2020-01-24 Namibia Case Study Highlights Importance of Data Policy Alignment for SDG 16.9) reported operating in 2020 and an [inter-ministry platform](2025-09-03 Season 3 - Namibia's Digital Identity Journey - From Vision to Reality (UNDP)) being deployed in 2025 are all the base holds.
developments:
The interoperability solution was delivered by an external academy with a technology partner on a project running to December 2016, and no operational status has been published since ([solution](2016-12-01 Governmental Interoperability in Namibia - E-riigi Akadeemia)).

The service bus was reported in a 2020 case study as linking electronic birth and death notification platforms to the population register, and no operational statement has been published since ([bus](2020-01-24 Namibia Case Study Highlights Importance of Data Policy Alignment for SDG 16.9)).

An inter-ministry data-exchange platform was named as being deployed in September 2025 with no record since ([platform](2025-09-03 Season 3 - Namibia's Digital Identity Journey - From Vision to Reality (UNDP))). Whether the three are the same system is not established, which is itself the state of the record.

summary: A [chipped electronic identity card](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026) with a ten-year validity is confirmed for September 2026, carrying a [randomly generated number](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026) for first-time applicants.
developments:
The card holds biometric and biographical data plus a digital identity component for remote authentication, with a thumbprint, a facial image and a personal identification number issued as on a bank card, and is valid for ten years against the indefinite lifespan of the document it replaces; a July 2026 launch was announced and slipped, cabinet approved the card in 2023, and none had been issued by August 2026 ([card](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026), [announcement](2025-06-09-namibia-to-launch-groundbreaking-e-id-namibiansun), [validity](2026-08-01-new-e-id-expiry-date-to-boost-security)).

Identity numbers had been derived from date of birth; first-time applicants will get a random number, with legacy numbers retained on the reverse of the card and existing documents valid until withdrawn by gazette notice ([number](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026), [account](2026-07-23-namibian-sun-govt-dismisses-mark-of-the-beast-eid)).

progress: Mixed, a school-based registration drive running while about a quarter of printed documents go uncollected
summary: [117,175 identity documents were issued in 2025](2026-03-16-namibia-expedites-electronic-ids-issuance-itweb), and [40,238 of 166,237 printed](2026-07-23-namibia-id-registration-taken-to-khomas-schools) were left uncollected over fifteen months.
developments:
The minister gave 117,175 national identity documents, 126,737 birth certificates and 682 refugee cards issued in 2025 ([issuance](2026-03-16-namibia-expedites-electronic-ids-issuance-itweb)); the 2024 comparator held in the base is a campaign count rather than an annual series ([issuance](2026-03-16-namibia-expedites-electronic-ids-issuance-itweb), [budget](2025-05-12 Namibia to step up civil registration efforts with $9M budget)).

Between April 2025 and June 2026, 166,237 documents were printed, 125,999 collected and 40,238 left uncollected, about a quarter of the print run ([uncollected](2026-07-23-namibia-id-registration-taken-to-khomas-schools)).

A school-based drive reached 24 of 55 target schools by July 2026, with officials returning to each school to hand printed documents to learners rather than requiring a ministry visit; documentary requirements are unchanged, which the source names as the residual barrier for learners with incomplete birth registration ([drive](2026-07-23-namibia-id-registration-taken-to-khomas-schools)).

summary: The [electronic identity is free at the point of issue](2026-07-29-namibian-home-affairs-clarifies-eid-costs) for first-time applicants, renewals, amendments and error replacements, with a first duplicate at N$150.
developments:
A first duplicate costs N$150 and a second N$300 ([fees](2026-07-29-namibian-home-affairs-clarifies-eid-costs)); the schedule was stated by ministry officials at Gobabis and on a regional awareness tour ([fees](2026-07-29-namibian-home-affairs-clarifies-eid-costs), [expiry](2026-08-01-new-e-id-expiry-date-to-boost-security)).

Free issue with a charge only for duplicates is the arrangement most likely to move the uncollected-document figure, and no fee for the card's digital component is separately stated.

summary: The [national population registration system](2025-09-03 Season 3 - Namibia's Digital Identity Journey - From Vision to Reality (UNDP)) has been operating since at least 2020 and is the register the September 2026 card is built on.
developments:
A 2021 baseline found obsolete software, siloed databases and little interoperability; the system now operates with remote biometric enrolment tested through hand-held devices ([system](2025-09-03 Season 3 - Namibia's Digital Identity Journey - From Vision to Reality (UNDP)), [case study](2020-01-24 Namibia Case Study Highlights Importance of Data Policy Alignment for SDG 16.9)).

No enrolment count, coverage share or performance figure is published for it, so the register underneath the country's identity programme is described and not measured.

progress: No change, no 2026/27 allocation published against the previous year's N$178.1m
summary: The civil registration department had [N$178,122,000 for 2025/26](2025-05-12 Namibia to step up civil registration efforts with $9M budget) and no 2026/27 allocation is on file.
developments:
A separate N$70m was allocated to the digital identity within a N$7.4bn ministry budget ([allocation](2025-04-29 Namibia prepares to roll out national digital ID system)).

No 2026/27 civil-registration allocation is on file ([budget](2025-05-12 Namibia to step up civil registration efforts with $9M budget)), which matters in the year the electronic card is to be issued and the school-based registration drive is running.

summary: A [Corporate Laws Bill](2025-10-07-bipa-corporate-laws-bill-2025-draft-3) at third draft would require every company to keep a beneficial-owner register in Namibia, above [existing online registration services](2026-07-16 The Home of Business and IP Registrations, Administration and Regulation in Namibia).
developments:
The draft consolidates and re-enacts the Companies Act with the business and intellectual property authority as registrar, and its clause 114 would require every company, and every external company establishing a place of business in the country, to keep a register of beneficial owners recording each owner's name, date of birth, identity-document number and residential, business, email and postal addresses; company process is routed through the electronic transactions statute ([bill](2025-10-07-bipa-corporate-laws-bill-2025-draft-3)).

Online name search, name reservation and application-status verification are already offered, with no transaction or uptake figure published ([services](2026-07-16 The Home of Business and IP Registrations, Administration and Regulation in Namibia)).

summary: The [Payment System Management Act 14 of 2023](2023-07-28 Namibia Payment System Management Act 14 of 2023) is in force, [licensing is moving to the central bank](2026-07-29-namibia-launches-instant-payments-system), and a [vision to 2030](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking) succeeds a strategy that [closed at 87 per cent implementation](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking).
developments:
The Act commenced in August 2023 and the payments association moved from a management council to a management board under it during 2025 ([Act](2023-07-28 Namibia Payment System Management Act 14 of 2023), [board](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking)).

Licensing and supervision of payment providers are to move to the central bank, with the association given independent governance and its own funding model; no instrument, commencement date or transition plan is published ([transfer](2026-07-29-namibia-launches-instant-payments-system)).

The 2021-2025 strategy closed at an 87 per cent average implementation rate over five years ([strategy](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking)), succeeded by a vision to 2030 whose next phase is in drafting on interoperable instant payments, the quick-response standard, open banking and cyber resilience ([vision](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking)).

summary: An [Instant Payment Solution](2026-07-29-namibia-launches-instant-payments-system) went live in June 2026 with three participating institutions, a [declaration of intent](2026-07-02-bon-ipn-namclear-instant-payments-pact-techafricanews) was signed on clearing integration, and a [quick-response standard](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking) is finalised.
developments:
The solution became operational in June 2026 after a live pilot, with a phased national rollout; the go-live month is stated by the central bank and no day is given ([launch](2026-07-29-namibia-launches-instant-payments-system), [build](2026-03-02 Namibia draws closer to instant government payments (IPS))).

A declaration of intent was signed by the central bank, the instant payments company and the clearing house to integrate instant payments with the national clearing infrastructure through the interbank settlement system, with no deliverables, funding or timetable published ([declaration](2026-07-02-bon-ipn-namclear-instant-payments-pact-techafricanews)).

The national quick-response payment standard is finalised with operationalisation named a priority and no live deployment reported ([standard](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking)).

summary: [Government-to-person social grants](2025-07-01-namibia-weighs-biometrics-instant-payment-biometricupdate) are the first use case named for the instant payment system, which went live in June 2026.
developments:
Biometric arrangements for the payment system were being weighed a year before it went live ([biometrics](2025-07-01-namibia-weighs-biometrics-instant-payment-biometricupdate)).

No grant volume, beneficiary count or disbursement figure through the system is published ([launch](2026-07-29-namibia-launches-instant-payments-system)), so the base records the channel that has been chosen for social transfers and not what has passed through it.

progress: No change, specifications complete with no implementation date published
summary: [Open banking specifications](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking) are complete, with implementation named a priority under the payments vision and no date published.
developments:
The specifications were reported completed in July 2026 through the payments association's annual report, which is not itself held ([specifications](2026-07-29-namibia-instant-payments-namqr-open-banking)).

No participating institution, interface standard or pilot is named. Completed specifications with no implementation date are the same shape as the quick-response standard beside them.

progress: Mixed, card e-commerce acceptance opened while participation in the continental settlement system remains unrecorded
summary: [Card e-commerce acceptance](2026-08-19-standard-bank-expands-unionpay-acceptance) opened to merchants in August 2026, while [participation in the continental payment and settlement system](2024-10-21 Namibia can benefit from Africa trade payment system (PAPSS)) is still not on record.
developments:
Online acceptance of an international card scheme opened to participating merchants, settling in local currency, dollars or both, as part of an extension to nine African markets; no country-specific merchant count is given ([acceptance](2026-08-19-standard-bank-expands-unionpay-acceptance), [extension](2026-08-19-tan-unionpay-standard-bank-nine-african-markets)).

A regional bank targeted central bank sign-up to the continental system by a Windhoek seminar in November 2024, and no record of Namibian participation exists at August 2026; about thirteen African central banks and 115 commercial banks were then on the platform ([system](2024-10-21 Namibia can benefit from Africa trade payment system (PAPSS))).

summary: Financial inclusion is put at [86 per cent for 2025](2026-07-29-namibia-launches-instant-payments-system), with an earlier 78 per cent figure dated to 2017 in one account and described as current in another.
developments:
The deputy governor gave 86 per cent at the payments association's annual general meeting, with the 78 per cent figure dated to 2017 ([rate](2026-07-29-namibia-launches-instant-payments-system)).

An industry executive had described the same 78 per cent as current in July 2025 ([executive](2025-07-01-namibia-weighs-biometrics-instant-payment-biometricupdate)). The two accounts date the same figure eight years apart, which is why the direction here is recorded and the size of the gain is not.

summary: [Banking fraud losses reached N$73.9m in 2025](2025-11-25-namibia-partners-with-banks-to-combat-fraud-itweb) against about N$8.7m a year in 2020, and a [fraud and cybersecurity summit](2025-11-25-namibia-partners-with-banks-to-combat-fraud-itweb) convened once.
developments:
Losses ran at about N$8.7m a year in 2020 on the central bank's figure and reached N$73.9m for 2025, with N$65m lost between January and October ([losses](2025-11-25-namibia-partners-with-banks-to-combat-fraud-itweb)); no 2026 figure is held ([losses](2025-11-25-namibia-partners-with-banks-to-combat-fraud-itweb)).

An inaugural summit was convened by the ICT ministry with the central bank, the bankers' association, the incident response team and an industry cyber council, and no second edition has been reported ([summit](2025-11-25-namibia-partners-with-banks-to-combat-fraud-itweb)).

summary: A [National Digital Health Policy 2026-2036](2026-02-06-who-afro-namibia-launches-national-digital-health-policy-2026-2036) was launched in February 2026, [succeeding a strategy whose period expired](2026-02-06-who-afro-namibia-launches-national-digital-health-policy-2026-2036), and a [community health application](2026-07-29-namibia-digital-community-system-health-rollout) is in preparation.
developments:
The ten-year policy was developed by the health ministry with international technical support, naming interoperability across health information systems, service delivery, governance and evidence-based decision-making as the problem it addresses; no funding, implementation plan or target is published, and it is known through a regional office's account rather than the ministry's own ([policy](2026-02-06-who-afro-namibia-launches-national-digital-health-policy-2026-2036)).

The 2021-2025 strategy's period expired at the end of 2025 and the successor followed five weeks later ([strategy](2021-01-01 Namibia National eHealth Strategy 2021-2025), [succession](2026-02-06-who-afro-namibia-launches-national-digital-health-policy-2026-2036)).

A mobile application for community health workers is in preparation with phased deployment and paper and digital running in parallel, after national training in July 2026; no rollout date is announced ([application](2026-07-29-namibia-digital-community-system-health-rollout)).

progress: Mixed, a roadmap target of digital identities for a quarter of the population by 2026 against card issuance beginning only in September and electronic signatures that missed their launch
summary: The [digital government roadmap](2026-02-10-towards-5g-enabled-digitalized-namibia-2026-telecomreviewafrica) targets digital identities for at least a quarter of the population by 2026, [electronic signatures](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026) missed a February 2026 launch, and [full digitisation is targeted for 2029/30](2025-08-24-namibia-25-new-network-towers-powercom-namibiansun).
developments:
The roadmap runs 2024-2026 and no digital-identity coverage figure has been published, with card issuance beginning only in September 2026; the document is known through one outlet's account ([roadmap](2026-02-10-towards-5g-enabled-digitalized-namibia-2026-telecomreviewafrica)).

Accreditation of electronic-signature service providers was under way with nationwide deployment targeted for February 2026; that target passed without a launch on record, and the capability is now described as a component of the September 2026 identity card ([signatures](2026-07-25-namibia-electronic-id-rollout-september-2026), [accreditation](2025-09-17-ai-abuse-overshadows-namibia-e-signature-drive-itweb)).

Full digitisation of government services is targeted for 2029/30 with no delivery measure published ([target](2025-08-24-namibia-25-new-network-towers-powercom-namibiansun)), and a N$13 million roads project control system was commissioned in August 2026 with no public access to its dashboard stated ([roads](2026-08-21-economist-namibia-road-network-digital-platform)).

summary: The capital adopted a [People-Centred Smart City Strategy 2026-2036](2026-06-16-cow-eyes-digital-makeover-with-rail-fibre-and-smart-city-push) in June 2026, with no funding requirement, timetable or institutional owner published.
developments:
The strategy was adopted by the city council in June 2026 and handed over in partnership with two United Nations bodies; the named projects are commercialisation of the city's own fibre network as the digital backbone and a proposed commuter rail ([strategy](2026-06-16-cow-eyes-digital-makeover-with-rail-fibre-and-smart-city-push), [reactions](2026-08-01-windhoeks-smart-city-vision-draws-mixed-reactions)).

A Chinese contribution to the pilot was acknowledged in July 2026 ([contribution](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure)), reported as CNY 98m and as N$245m with no dated conversion between them ([concerns](2026-08-04-namibia-mp-data-control-concerns-china-smart-city-grant)); smart-city development had been under discussion since 2025 with no instrument published ([discussion](2025-09-23-namibia-expedites-data-centre-smart-city-development-itweb)).

summary: [21 of 188 schools in one region have workable connectivity](2026-08-19-thevillager-kavango-schools-poor-network-coverage), leaving 55,002 learners without digital teaching tools, against a national figure of [339 schools and 50 health centres](2025-06-04 Namibia targets 100% telecom coverage nationwide by 2030) lacking adequate connectivity.
developments:
The regional education directors told the parliamentary ICT committee that 21 of Kavango West's 188 schools have workable connectivity, leaving 55,002 learners without digital teaching tools, and that the neighbouring region's 197 schools serving 86,282 learners are only marginally connected ([committee](2026-08-19-thevillager-kavango-schools-poor-network-coverage)); health officials told the same committee that clinics still struggle with unreliable coverage ([committee](2026-08-19-thevillager-kavango-schools-poor-network-coverage), [schools](2026-08-11-namibia-kavango-west-schools-internet-access), [clinics](2026-08-11-namibia-kavango-west-health-network-coverage)).

The ministry's national figure of 339 schools and 50 health centres lacking adequate connectivity dates from June 2025 with no later official figure; a research council account records 65.4 per cent of schools connected in 2023, 1,311 of 2,004, on a different basis that is not comparable ([national](2025-06-04 Namibia targets 100% telecom coverage nationwide by 2030), [council](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc)).

summary: Cabinet [ordered a N$39.5m artificial-intelligence crop-monitoring contract cancelled](2026-08-24-namibian-sun-govt-weighs-action-official-n40m-ai-deal) in August 2026, weeks after the [one-year contract was reported](2026-08-17-namibia-agriculture-ai-deal-6th-grain-transparency).
developments:
The contract, in effect from June 2026, was to build a national crop-monitoring system using satellite imagery, geospatial analysis and artificial intelligence to map agricultural land, monitor crop and pasture health and forecast five crops, with software, models and technical expertise transferred to the ministry and officials trained to run it independently ([contract](2026-08-17-namibia-agriculture-ai-deal-6th-grain-transparency)).

Cabinet ordered it cancelled in the week of 17 August 2026 and the agriculture ministry is weighing action against the official who authorised it; government did not attribute the cancellation to the technology, the value is reported as N$39.5m and N$40m in different accounts, and the review itself is not published ([cancellation](2026-08-24-namibian-sun-govt-weighs-action-official-n40m-ai-deal), [block](2026-08-20-namibian-cabinet-blocks-us-ai-crop-monitoring-tender), [account](2026-08-19-observer24-namibia-cancels-agriculture-ai-deal)).

The award had drawn public objection over transparency and local participation, and no procurement route or text of the data-ownership terms was published.

summary: Namibia is one of five backing governments in a [pan-African language artificial-intelligence initiative](2026-07-31-gsma-atlas-umoja-ai-launch), and an [indigenous-language voice repository](2026-08-13-namibia-undp-digital-innovation-youth-day) is under construction.
developments:
The initiative was launched at a continental telecommunications conference with the ICT ministry a named partner, scaling an existing national model template; the stated commitment is ministerial support rather than a named contribution, and no Namibian funding, dataset or deliverable is published ([initiative](2026-07-31-gsma-atlas-umoja-ai-launch), [declaration](2026-07-24-gsma-abuja-declaration-meaningful-connectivity-atlas-umoja), [account](2026-07-28-la-gsma-lance-une-initiative-pour-developper-l-ia-en-langues-africaines)).

A voice-data repository for Namibian indigenous languages is being built through a development programme sprint with the national science and technology university; no language count, corpus size, licence or release date is stated, and who owns the collected speech and on what terms it can train models is not addressed ([repository](2026-08-13-namibia-undp-digital-innovation-youth-day)).

summary: The [first privately owned mobile network](2025-09-04-paratus-launches-namibia-first-private-mobile-network-connectingafrica) launched in September 2025 on [N$600m of investment](2025-09-04-paratus-launches-namibia-first-private-mobile-network-connectingafrica), against a [dominance determination](2024-08-15-namibia-gg-8416-gn-456-cran-determination-of-dominant-position-telecommunications) naming the state operator dominant in all four priority markets.
developments:
The network is live on long-term evolution and 5G, with N$600m invested in the preceding year and N$1.42bn in Namibian network infrastructure since 2018, company-reported ([launch](2025-09-04-paratus-launches-namibia-first-private-mobile-network-connectingafrica), [announcement](2025-08-19-paratus-to-launch-mobile-network-namibiansun), [investment](2025-09-04-paratus-launches-namibia-first-private-mobile-network-connectingafrica), [record](2025-01-01-paratus-nam-2025-namibia-private-mobile-network-bw05)).

The 2024 determination names the state fixed operator dominant in all four priority markets, alone in wired end-user access and jointly elsewhere, with termination treated as a natural monopoly; the regulator describes its approach across all three exercises as one of minimal intervention ([determination](2024-08-15-namibia-gg-8416-gn-456-cran-determination-of-dominant-position-telecommunications)).

summary: A [national artificial-intelligence institute](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc) recommended by a 2022 task force is proposed and not established, with no site, budget, host or founding instrument on file.
developments:
The sixth national development plan calls for a research centre and the institute remains proposed ([institute](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc)).

Four years after the recommendation there is no site, budget, host or founding instrument. The working capability the country has instead sits in a university accelerator recorded separately.

progress: No change, a fund authorised at US$20m with no manager, close or disbursement on file
summary: Cabinet authorised an [information technology venture capital fund at US$20m](2025-09-23-namibia-expedites-data-centre-smart-city-development-itweb) and directed engagement with female founders as potential beneficiaries.
developments:
No fund manager, first close, instrument, Namibian-dollar figure or disbursement is on file eleven months later ([fund](2025-09-23-namibia-expedites-data-centre-smart-city-development-itweb)).

The amount is published only in United States dollars, so the row cannot carry the announcing party's own currency, and no count of firms, deals or jobs is held for the country.

summary: An [Information and Communication syllabus](2024-12-01-nied-information-and-communication-syllabus-grade-8-9) is compulsory and assessable across Grades 4 to 12, and a [learning platform](2026-08-13-namibia-learning-passport-unicef) launched in August 2026.
developments:
The subject runs across three themes of digital, media and information literacy; the Grade 12 syllabus was published in 2018 for implementation in 2021 and the Grade 8 and 9 syllabus in December 2024 for phased implementation in 2025 and 2026 ([syllabus](2024-12-01-nied-information-and-communication-syllabus-grade-8-9), [senior secondary](2018-01-01-nied-information-and-communication-syllabus-grade-12)).

A digital and offline learning platform aimed at rural, remote and underserved young people was launched by the education ministry with an international agency; no user target, content catalogue, device requirement or offline distribution route is stated ([platform](2026-08-13-namibia-learning-passport-unicef)).

summary: No standalone national digital-literacy strategy or programme exists [outside the school curriculum](2024-12-01-nied-information-and-communication-syllabus-grade-8-9).
developments:
The Information and Communication subject is the country's whole digital-literacy provision on this record, compulsory and assessable for school pupils and reaching nobody else ([curriculum](2024-12-01-nied-information-and-communication-syllabus-grade-8-9)).

No adult programme, measurement or target is held. The identity awareness campaign and the youth ambassador programme recorded elsewhere in this ledger are the nearest thing to population-level digital outreach, and both are about one credential.

summary: A [public-service cyber training partnership](2026-06-09-nipam-global-cybersecurity-centre-partnership-techafricanews) was signed in June 2026 for joint training of public servants, extending to private-sector professionals.
developments:
No funding, cohort size or delivery date is published, and the memorandum text is not held ([partnership](2026-06-09-nipam-global-cybersecurity-centre-partnership-techafricanews)).

It sits beside a cabinet-approved cyber-skills programme for government technology staff that has also not reported a cohort, so the civil service has two approved training routes and no trained count.

summary: A [university artificial-intelligence and robotics accelerator](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc) underpins the country's first artificial-intelligence degree, and a [five-node computing cluster](2026-08-09-inceit-param-hpc-nust-namibia-specification) is specified for a university campus.
developments:
The accelerator was launched with central bank funding and supports bachelor's and honours degrees in artificial intelligence and a master's in data science; it is known through the research council's authors citing the university's own announcement ([accelerator](2026-02-16-namibia-building-ai-readiness-coordination-collaboration-isc)).

A five-node high-performance computing cluster is specified for deployment at the science and technology university under a bilateral centre of excellence, with no operator, cost or opening date published; it is a university research cluster and the source itself warns it must not be conflated with a national facility ([cluster](2026-08-09-inceit-param-hpc-nust-namibia-specification)).

summary: [Twenty-five towers](2025-08-24-namibia-25-new-network-towers-powercom-namibiansun) entered service across nine regions, [schools and clinics under new towers get seven years free internet](2026-01-27 Namibian schools, clinics to get free internet), and [100 per cent coverage is targeted for 2030](2025-06-04 Namibia targets 100% telecom coverage nationwide by 2030).
developments:
Twenty-five towers went into service across nine regions at N$40m in total, about N$1.6m each, built with the state fixed operator ([towers](2025-08-24-namibia-25-new-network-towers-powercom-namibiansun)).

Schools and clinics under towers built in the previous two years get free internet for seven years, on N$80m in nine radio access network towers over two years ([free internet](2026-01-27 Namibian schools, clinics to get free internet)); no list or count of covered schools or clinics is published ([free internet](2026-01-27 Namibian schools, clinics to get free internet)).

The 2030 coverage target was set in June 2025 against about 360,000 people, roughly 12 per cent, outside 4G coverage at February 2024, with a parallel internet-use target of 53 to 90 per cent by 2030 ([target](2025-06-04 Namibia targets 100% telecom coverage nationwide by 2030), [plan](2026-02-10-towards-5g-enabled-digitalized-namibia-2026-telecomreviewafrica)). Siting delays on communal land are the constraint the ministry names, and it met the traditional authorities' trust with the regulator and three operators in July 2026 with no agreement reported ([siting](2026-07-30-namibia-taps-chiefs-for-network-rollout)).

summary: [682 refugee identity cards](2026-03-16-namibia-expedites-electronic-ids-issuance-itweb) were issued in 2025, and [cash assistance through mobile money](2025-02-01 Cash-Based Interventions provide a ray of hope for refugees in Namibia amid severe drought and funding shortages) reached about 6,000 people in 2025.
developments:
Issuance of refugee cards began in June 2024 and 682 were issued in calendar 2025 ([cards](2026-03-16-namibia-expedites-electronic-ids-issuance-itweb), [system](2024-09-09 Namibia's new CRVS, national ID system reflects key data protection aspects)).

Cash assistance through mobile money launched in February 2025 for about 6,000 individuals in over 1,000 households, with the agency reporting it held 40 per cent of the resources needed and no record since ([assistance](2025-02-01 Cash-Based Interventions provide a ray of hope for refugees in Namibia amid severe drought and funding shortages)).

summary: An [electronic identity awareness campaign](2026-07-29-namibia-eid-community-outreach-omaheke-undp) is running region by region in local languages, with a [youth ambassadors programme](2026-08-13-namibia-undp-digital-innovation-youth-day) promoting take-up.
developments:
The campaign opened in the capital region and its Omaheke leg ran across all seven constituencies in late July and early August 2026, run by home affairs with a development agency and the regulator, with a brand ambassador running sessions in local languages ([campaign](2026-07-29-namibia-eid-community-outreach-omaheke-undp), [conference](2025-06-09-namibia-to-launch-groundbreaking-e-id-namibiansun), [preparation](2026-07-28-namibia-steps-up-digital-id-campaign-ahead-of-september-rollout)).

A youth ambassadors programme uses young people to promote take-up and civic participation; participant numbers, cost, duration and any enrolment effect are not stated, and the funding agency's own account is the only source ([ambassadors](2026-08-13-namibia-undp-digital-innovation-youth-day)).

summary: A [national strategy for the development of statistics](2023-02-01-namibia-nsds-2023-24-2026-27) runs 2023/24 to 2026/27 at N$58,995,000, alongside the agency's own [institutional strategic plan](2022-04-01-namibia-statistics-agency-strategic-plan-2022-2027).
developments:
The strategy sets four goals covering better use of statistics for policy, efficient data processes, a better funded national statistics system and improved integration with spatial data, resting on ten first-phase sector plans, at a total implementation cost of N$58,995,000 over four years ([strategy](2023-02-01-namibia-nsds-2023-24-2026-27)).

The agency's separate institutional plan covers 2022/23 to 2026/27 on four focus areas including spatial data coordination and alternative data sources, and records that funding was relatively adequate until about 2016 and that the population census slipped twice for want of funds ([plan](2022-04-01-namibia-statistics-agency-strategic-plan-2022-2027)). The two are distinct documents and should not be merged.

summary: The [2023 population and housing census](2026-07-27-namibia-bon-eid-administrative-data-sharing-census-costs) was the country's first fully digital census and remains the reference count at 3,022,401.
developments:
It is cited by the statistics agency as a step in modernising the national statistical system ([census](2026-07-27-namibia-bon-eid-administrative-data-sharing-census-costs), [awareness](2026-07-30-namibia-bon-nsa-statistics-awareness-day-admin-records-ai)).

The agency's own institutional plan records that the census slipped from August 2021 and again from August 2022 for want of funds, so the digital operation was delivered two years late and no successor is scheduled on this record.

summary: The [producer price index moved off spreadsheets](2026-08-25-namibian-new-system-rewrites-producer-price-data) onto an automated engine with revisions back to 2015, and the [quarterly bulletin](2026-08-21-nsa-namibia-producer-price-index-bulletin-q2-2026) is now held as a primary.
developments:
Compilation moved to an automated processing engine, disclosed in the second-quarter 2026 bulletin and carrying retrospective revisions of producer price estimates back to 2015: missing prices are now imputed as a turnover-weighted average of observed price relatives within the product group, imputation is capped at three consecutive periods before an item must be replaced, and automated validation flags extreme swings and entry errors ([system](2026-08-25-namibian-new-system-rewrites-producer-price-data)).

The bulletin itself is held in full where the base had carried its figures only as reported, and it carries no digital-sector breakout ([bulletin](2026-08-21-nsa-namibia-producer-price-index-bulletin-q2-2026)).

The country has subscribed to an international data dissemination standard since December 2022, one of about seven African countries ([subscription](2026-07-27-namibia-bon-eid-administrative-data-sharing-census-costs)), and held an inaugural statistics awareness day in July 2026 themed on statistics in the digital age ([day](2026-07-30-namibia-bon-nsa-statistics-awareness-day-admin-records-ai)).

progress: Mixed, an agency microdata catalogue with stated access terms against two new platforms that publish nothing
summary: The statistics agency runs [data portals and a microdata catalogue](2026-08-09-namibia-statistics-agency-data-portals-microdata-catalogue) of sixteen studies with stated access terms, while a [reporting application](2026-08-14-namibia-citymender-infrastructure-reporting-app) and an [environmental platform](2026-08-07-namibia-mea-monitoring-platform-gef-undp) publish no dataset.
developments:
The agency operates a data portals page and a catalogue holding sixteen Namibian studies from 1992 to 2023, each carrying a stated access term; the source states explicitly that this is agency-run dissemination and not a government-wide open data policy or portal, which the base does not hold for the country ([catalogue](2026-08-09-namibia-statistics-agency-data-portals-microdata-catalogue)).

An infrastructure reporting application launched nationwide takes public reports of more than thirty kinds of fault onto a mapped national dataset with automatic facial and licence-plate redaction; it is privately built and privately held, with no user count, data-sharing arrangement with any authority, or licence for the dataset stated ([application](2026-08-14-namibia-citymender-infrastructure-reporting-app)).

An environmental agreements monitoring platform launched at N$12m to centralise environmental data for planning and national reporting, with no public access, dataset list, licence or publication rule stated, so it is a reporting tool rather than open data on the record held ([platform](2026-08-07-namibia-mea-monitoring-platform-gef-undp)).

summary: A [satellite data-receiving ground station](2026-02-13 Namibia gets  Chinese satellite ground station) is in operation, the country's first, and a [Space Science and Technology Bill](2026-02-13 Namibia gets  Chinese satellite ground station) has been approved for drafting with no text published.
developments:
The station was handed over by China at the earth station outside Windhoek and receives remote-sensing data, operated by fourteen trained Namibians ([station](2026-02-13 Namibia gets  Chinese satellite ground station), [handover](2026-08-04-namibia-mp-data-control-concerns-china-smart-city-grant)).

Cabinet approved drafting of a space statute during 2025 and no text or introduction date has been published ([bill](2026-02-13 Namibia gets  Chinese satellite ground station), [approval](2026-02-13 Namibia gets  Chinese satellite ground station)).

The country's one recorded application of satellite data to agriculture, a crop-monitoring contract, was cancelled by cabinet in August 2026.

summary: A [subsea cable landing at Swakopmund](2026-02-19-grounding-the-cloud-in-namibia-namibiansun) has been in service since 2022 and is the only United States technology asset in the country the base carries outside satellite licensing.
developments:
The landing is cited as the connectivity leg of the case for hosting compute in the country ([landing](2026-02-19-grounding-the-cloud-in-namibia-namibiansun), [ownership](2025-10-20 Redefining competition and submarine cable ownership Equiano, MainOne, and the making of middlemen)).

No hyperscaler memorandum, region, data centre or commitment is recorded, and the one American satellite operator to apply for a licence was refused. So the relationship is a cable and a refusal.

summary: China committed [CNY 98,000,000 to the capital smart-city pilot](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure), is [building a data centre for artificial-intelligence workloads](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure) and handed over the country's [first satellite ground station](2026-08-04-namibia-mp-data-control-concerns-china-smart-city-grant).
developments:
The commitment, about US$14.4m on the source's conversion, covers digital infrastructure, artificial-intelligence capability and skills under the city's ten-year strategy ([commitment](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure)); the signature date is padded from a reference to the end of June, and an opposition member gives the same commitment as N$245m ([commitment](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure), [talks](2026-07-08-nandi-ndaitwah-pushes-ai-jobs-huawei-talks-namibian), [record](2026-01-01-government-of-china-nam-2026-windhoek-smart-city-bw14)).

A vendor is building smart-city solutions and a data centre with two ministries, with no signed agreement, annexure or contractor list held ([data centre](2026-07-08 China funds Namibia digital infrastructure)).

The satellite ground station outside the capital was handed over by China and is operated by fourteen trained Namibians ([station](2026-08-04-namibia-mp-data-control-concerns-china-smart-city-grant)). An opposition member has raised data-control concerns about the smart-city grant.

summary: The [European indicative programme](2024-01-01-eu-amending-decision-mip-2021-2027-sub-saharan-africa-annex-c2024-7502) has no digital priority area, allocating EUR 26,000,000 for 2025-2027 with digitalisation only cross-cutting.
developments:
The initial 2021-2024 envelope was an indicative EUR 37,000,000, and the mid-term review set the 2025-2027 allocation at EUR 26,000,000: inclusive green growth twenty, good governance and gender equality two, support measures four, and foundational skills education nil ([amendment](2024-01-01-eu-amending-decision-mip-2021-2027-sub-saharan-africa-annex-c2024-7502), [programme](2021-01-01-eu-multi-annual-indicative-programme-2021-2027-namibia-annex)).

The named digital offer is support to Parliament's electronic-parliament blueprint, and data protection and cyber security appear once in the programme, qualified as possible.

summary: A [bilateral economic commission](2026-02-19-nipdb-namibia-uae-business-forum) with technology transfer and skills in its remit was proposed at a business forum in February 2026, with no agreement signed.
developments:
The commission's proposed remit covers technology transfer, skills development, industrialisation and manufacturing, and the Gulf side raised investment protection and double-taxation agreements; no Gulf-state digital, data-centre or artificial-intelligence agreement is published ([proposal](2026-02-19-nipdb-namibia-uae-business-forum)).

The forum's own trade list runs to diamonds, scrap metal, charcoal, frozen fish and dates, with the ask being value addition before export, which is the context the technology element sits inside.

summary: A [cyber security memorandum](2025-07-10-namibia-india-cyber-security-alliance-itweb) was signed in July 2025 and [cooperation was advanced at a joint trade committee](2026-08-12-namibia-india-cybersecurity-digital-ties) in August 2026.
developments:
The memorandum was signed at State House during a visit, alongside an entrepreneurship centre agreement, and no implementation activity, funding or programme has been reported since ([memorandum](2025-07-10-namibia-india-cyber-security-alliance-itweb)).

Cooperation was advanced at the fourth joint trade committee in New Delhi in August 2026, building on a memorandum signed by the two heads of government in July 2025, with bilateral trade put at more than US$592m in 2025/26 ([committee](2026-08-12-namibia-india-cybersecurity-digital-ties)); the memorandum text is not held and no workstream, funding or timetable is attached ([committee](2026-08-12-namibia-india-cybersecurity-digital-ties)).

A five-node computing cluster is separately specified for a university campus under a bilateral centre of excellence ([cluster](2026-08-09-inceit-param-hpc-nust-namibia-specification)).
